In Spain, many children get their presents not at Christmas but on 6 January, from the Three Wise Men. People eat “roscón de Reyes”, a ring cake with a little figurine hidden inside.
For several days the streets of Valencia fill with giant figures made of cardboard and wood, the “fallas”. On the night of 19 March, at “la cremà”, almost all of them are burned.
In Catalonia, on St George’s Day, people give each other a rose and a book. 23 April is also the day the death of Cervantes is remembered.
From 7 July, every morning at “el encierro”, people run through the streets ahead of the bulls. Everyone wears white with a red scarf.
On the last Wednesday of August, thousands of people pelt each other with tomatoes in the streets of the little town of Buñol for an hour.
On the night of 15 to 16 September, the president repeats “el Grito” from the balcony, and the crowd shouts “¡Viva México!”.
On 12 October 1492, Columbus’s ships reached America. Today it is a day for the Spanish-speaking world, for its nearly 500 million native speakers of Spanish.
On 1 and 2 November, Mexicans joyfully remember their loved ones who have died: they build altars with orange flowers, candles, photos and “pan de muerto”.
“Nochebuena” means “the Good Night”: the family has dinner together, and in many Latin American countries presents are opened at midnight.
It is the Spanish-speaking world’s “1 April”: on 28 December people play pranks, called “inocentadas”, and even newspapers publish fake news as a joke.
At midnight Spaniards eat 12 grapes, one for each chime of the clock at Puerta del Sol. If you manage it, you’ll have luck all year.
It is the most important holiday: the family eats “おせち”, children receive money in envelopes, “お年玉” (otoshidama), and people visit a shrine or temple.
On the second Monday of January, young people who have become adults attend ceremonies in kimonos and smart suits.
People throw soybeans around the house shouting “鬼は外、福は内” (Demons out, good luck in!).
Families with little girls display dolls dressed as an ancient imperial court and wish them health and luck.
Around late March and early April, the Japanese picnic under the blossoming cherry trees. TV channels report the “cherry-blossom front” every day.
Carp-shaped streamers, “こいのぼり”, fly above houses: the carp swimming upstream against the current is a symbol of strength.
Legend says two lovers separated by the Milky Way meet once a year. People write their wishes on paper strips, “たんざく”, and hang them on bamboo.
Around mid-August, the Japanese go home to their families to honour their ancestors; lanterns are lit and people dance the “ぼんおどり”.
Children aged 3, 5 and 7 are taken to the shrine in traditional clothes and receive “ちとせあめ”, long “thousand-year” candies.
People eat soba noodles for a long life, and temple bells ring 108 times, “除夜の鐘”, to drive away the 108 earthly desires.
On the night of 5 to 6 January, a kind old witch, “la Befana”, flies on her broomstick and fills children’s stockings with sweets. Naughty ones get “carbone”, (sugar) coal.
On 25 April, Italy celebrates the end of the occupation in the Second World War; “Bella ciao” is often sung.
On 2 June 1946, Italians voted to become a republic. Military planes draw the green-white-red flag, “il Tricolore”, in the sky.
On 2 July and 16 August, the districts of Siena compete in a horse race lasting about 90 seconds around the Piazza del Campo.
The name comes from Latin “Feriae Augusti”, the holidays of Emperor Augustus. Today almost all of Italy heads to the sea.

Italians make “il presepe”, a nativity scene with figurines, and eat “panettone” or “pandoro”. The proverb says “Natale con i tuoi, Pasqua con chi vuoi”: Christmas with your family, Easter with whoever you like.
